title: Physical activity and global DNA methylation in healthy adults: a cross-sectional study
content:
Abstract
Physical activity has been associated with changes in DNA methylation, an epigenetic modification involved in gene regulation and genomic stability. However, evidence concerning its association with global DNA methylation in peripheral blood remains limited. Global DNA methylation measurements also differ from DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks and cannot directly estimate biological age. This comparative cross-sectional study included 120 healthy Jordanian adults classified as physically active (n = 60) or sedentary (n = 60). Global DNA methylation levels were measured in peripheral blood leukocyte DNA using an ELISA-based assay and expressed as relative 5-methylcytosine (5-mC) levels. Between-group comparisons, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI) were performed. Physically active participants had higher mean global DNA methylation levels than sedentary participants (4.8 ± 0.6 vs. 3.6 ± 0.7, P < .001; Cohen’s d = 1.84). Weekly exercise duration was positively correlated with global DNA methylation (r = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.38–0.66, P < .001). In the adjusted regression model, exercise duration remained positively associated with global DNA methylation (β = 0.150, P < .001), while age showed a modest negative association (β = −0.18, P = .037). Leukocyte subtype composition and quantitative dietary intake were not assessed. Habitual physical activity was associated with higher global DNA methylation levels in healthy adults. These findings do not establish causality or demonstrate slower biological aging. Further studies incorporating leukocyte composition, dietary assessment, and site-specific methylation analyses are needed to clarify the biological significance of this association.
